title: Rome's 'justified by works too': moral conditions + infused virtues God will crown
source_text: LVI. Quum vero Scholae Romanae Theologi affirmant nos, non fide sola, sed operibus quoque justificari, sententia eorum est, non solum credendi actum, praecise consideratum, sed multos alios, quales sunt timor judicii divini, dolor de peccato, ejus detestatio, propositum novae vitae, spes misericordiae a Deo obtinendae, & inde oriens Dei amor & dilectio, & si qui sunt istiusmodi, esse morales dispositiones, id est, conditiones quae, ex ordine a Deo constituto, in nobis praecedere debent remissionem peccatorum, & renovationem internam per Spiritum Sanctum; & sine quibus Deus non solet gratiam istam nobis largiri. Deinde cum fide virtutes caeteras, constituere veri nominis justitiam, a qua fideles in Scriptura sancti justique nuncupantur: & quam etiam Deus judicio suo comprobabit, quum illam in ultimo die vita aeterna remunerabitur: quorum utrumque patet ex ante dictis a Theologis Reformatis concedi. Adeo ut hactenus hic de vocibus tantum, non de reipsa contendi videatur.
pass_a_gloss: But when the theologians of the Roman School affirm that we are justified not by faith alone but by works also, their opinion is that not only the act of believing precisely considered, but many others—such as fear of divine judgment, sorrow for sin, detestation of it, purpose of a new life, hope of mercy to be obtained from God, and the love of God arising thence, and if there are any of that kind—are moral dispositions, that is, conditions which by the order constituted by God ought to precede in us the remission of sins and interior renovation through the Holy Spirit; and without which God is not wont to bestow that grace on us. Next, that with faith the other virtues constitute righteousness worthy of the name, by which the faithful in Scripture are called holy and just: and which God also will approve in his judgment when on the last day he will reward it with eternal life: both of which it is clear from what was said above are conceded by the Reformed theologians. So that thus far the contention here seems only about words, not about the thing itself.
pass_b_english: Rome's 'works justify' = repentant moral conditions before grace, plus infused virtues God will crown.
Reformed already concede both; so far the fight looks verbal.
